neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis — complete inability to open eyelids voluntarily without assistance. On attempted upward gaze, minimal voluntary lid elevation. Pupils equal, round, reactive bilaterally. Extraocular movements FULL in all directions — NO ophthalmoplegia. No diplopia. Bell's phenomenon preserved. No facial weakness. No dysarthria. Gag preserved.
neurological_exam.motor: Upper extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally. Lower extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally. Normal bulk and tone throughout.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact light touch, pinprick, vibration, proprioception in all extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Global areflexia — absent biceps, brachioradialis, triceps, patellar, Achilles bilaterally. Plantars downgoing.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin intact. No ataxia.
neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 3.4 L (predicted 3.6 L — 94%). NIF: -48 cmH2O. No diurnal variation in ptosis. Ptosis progressed from left eye to bilateral over 5 days. No fatigability on sustained upgaze. No preceding illness recalled by patient.

patient.chief_complaint: Seven-day progressive bilateral ptosis with complete inability to open eyes, preserved eye movements, no limb weakness, global areflexia.
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. K. is a 33-year-old teacher presenting with a 7-day history of progressive bilateral ptosis. The ptosis began in the left eye and spread to involve the right eye 5 days later. She now has nearly complete bilateral ptosis and cannot open her eyelids voluntarily without using her fingers. She reports mild generalized malaise and fatigue with routine activities over the same period. She denies any diplopia — eye movements are fully intact. She has no difficulty swallowing, speaking, or breathing. She notes no weakness in her arms or legs and was able to walk to the emergency department without difficulty. She has no sensory symptoms. There is no diurnal variation in her ptosis — it does not improve in the morning or worsen with prolonged activity. There is no prior history of similar symptoms. She recalls no recent respiratory illness, gastrointestinal illness, or other viral syndrome preceding the onset. She denies exposure to spoiled food, wounds, or ticks. She takes no medications. The initial concern was myasthenia gravis given the bilateral ptosis, but the absence of diurnal variation and preservation of full extraocular movements with global areflexia on exam is atypical for classic MG. The global areflexia in the absence of any weakness is the key distinguishing finding.

specialized_test.test_type: Nerve Conduction Studies, EMG, and Repetitive Nerve Stimulation

findings.finding: DML 5.6 ms (prolonged); CV 42 m/s (borderline); CMAP 4.8 mV
Absent bilateral median; absent bilateral peroneal
No decremental response — RNS negative. Excludes neuromuscular junction disorder.
Normal jitter — NMJ transmission normal. Excludes myasthenia gravis.

quantitative_data.pattern: Mild demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with absent F-waves — consistent with GBS presenting as isolated ptosis with areflexia (cranial nerve variant)

specialized_test.impression: Electrophysiology confirms peripheral nervous system involvement: absent F-waves and H-reflex with borderline DML prolongation. Repetitive nerve stimulation and single-fiber EMG negative — NMJ transmission normal, excludes MG and Lambert-Eaton definitively. Pattern meets GBS criteria. Isolated ptosis with global areflexia and early demyelination represents a rare GBS variant — the cranial neuropathy (levator palpebrae) preceded limb involvement.
recommended_actions: Edrophonium (Tensilon) test not required — NMJ testing already negative

ecg.interpretation: Normal ECG. Minimal autonomic involvement at this stage.

output.interpretation: Opening pressure: 132 mmH2O. WBC: 3 cells/mm3 (N/A PMN/N/A lymph). Protein: 62 mg/dL (elevated). Glucose: 65 mg/dL (ratio 0.72). Gram stain: No organisms. Cultures: No growth. VDRL: Non-reactive.

output.impression: Normal MRI brain. No structural or demyelinating cause for bilateral ptosis identified. No Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis signal changes. Normal brainstem excludes central cause.
recommended_actions: Structural central cause excluded — supports peripheral GBS cranial variant diagnosis

findings: No autonomic dysfunction at this stage
output.impression: Minimal autonomic involvement. General ward monitoring appropriate. Escalate if FVC declines or arrhythmias develop.

findings.finding: No improvement in ptosis with edrophonium 10 mg IV — test NEGATIVE

quantitative_data.result: Negative — no pharmacological improvement in ptosis

output.impression: Edrophonium challenge test negative. Does not support myasthenia gravis. Combined with negative RNS and negative MG antibodies, MG is effectively excluded.
recommended_actions: MG excluded — proceed with GBS management

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, cranial nerve variant — isolated bilateral ptosis with global areflexia (seronegative, anti-GQ1b negative)

differential.key_features: No diurnal variation; AChR/MuSK/LRP4 all negative; RNS no decrement; edrophonium negative; global areflexia atypical for MG
No ophthalmoplegia; no ataxia; anti-GQ1b negative; ptosis without EOM involvement
Pupils reactive and symmetric; no autonomic dysfunction; no exposure history; RNS negative
Alert with normal higher functions; normal brain MRI; no hypersomnolence

optimal_actions.action: Serial FVC/NIF — cranial GBS can progress

critical_actions: Recognize GBS presenting as isolated bilateral ptosis with global areflexia — ptosis without weakness can be GBS
Global areflexia is the key distinguishing finding — MG does NOT cause areflexia
RNS and single-fiber EMG needed to exclude NMJ disorder before diagnosing GBS
Anti-GQ1b negative — distinguishes from Miller Fisher syndrome (which has ophthalmoplegia anyway)
Edrophonium challenge negative — definitively excludes MG
Seronegative GBS (no ganglioside antibodies) does not change management — IVIG still indicated
contraindicated_actions: Pyridostigmine for presumed MG without NMJ testing confirmation
Discharging without monitoring — cranial GBS can progress to respiratory failure
key_reasoning_points: Bilateral ptosis with FULL extraocular movements and preserved pupillary responses — ophthalmoplegia (from CN III, IV, VI) is NOT present; this is NOT Miller Fisher syndrome
Global areflexia in the absence of limb weakness is a cardinal feature of this GBS cranial variant — MG does not cause areflexia
CSF albumino-cytologic dissociation in the first week is unusual for Miller Fisher — this favored atypical GBS
Anti-GQ1b is typically absent in cases with ptosis alone without ophthalmoplegia (GQ1b is concentrated at the NMJ of EOM)
GBS can present with isolated cranial nerve involvement — recognition requires testing NCS/EMG to find peripheral demyelination

red_herrings.intended_effect: Immediately suggest myasthenia gravis as diagnosis, leading to MG-focused workup before GBS is considered
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Global areflexia on exam is the key — MG does not cause areflexia; the reflexes must be tested before fixating on MG

red_herrings.data_point: No diurnal variation mentioned but fatigability not assessed on initial triage
red_herrings.intended_effect: Leave open the possibility of fatigable MG
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Systematic NMJ testing (RNS, single-fiber EMG, edrophonium, antibody panel) comprehensively excludes MG regardless of fatigability history

metadata.difficulty_description: Isolated bilateral ptosis as sole cranial nerve manifestation of GBS — closely mimics myasthenia gravis; global areflexia is the discriminating finding
